```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(ADMIT)
```

## The problem

Admixture mapping regresses a trait on local ancestry, so what each individual contributes is the
*variance* their local ancestry has across the genome: `2q(1-q)`, which vanishes as they approach
unadmixed. The caller's error does not vanish. A truly unadmixed individual still receives invented
focal tracts at a rate `eps0` that barely depends on who they are.

So reliability is

```{r}
q <- 10^seq(-4, -0.5, length.out = 200)
plot(q, adm_reliability(q, eps0 = 1.4e-3), type = "l", log = "x", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "global focal ancestry q", ylab = "reliability")
```

and it collapses exactly where most of a biobank's nominally-admixed individuals sit. Including them
adds people, not information. That is why a threshold has to exist, and the package's job is to put
it somewhere defensible rather than at a round number.

## Step 1 — measure your own caller's floor

`eps0` is what your caller reports for the focal ancestry in people who carry none of it. You do not
need a simulation: any biobank contains individuals who are near-pure in some *other* ancestry.

```{r eval = FALSE}
eps <- adm_eps0(global_Q, local_dosage = my_dosage, focal = "AFR", pure_cut = 0.99)
eps
#> Background false-call rate for focal AFR
#>   eps0 = 0.000587   (sd across the reference group 0.000825)
#>   reference: 39,069 of 52,639 individuals, >99% in a single non-focal ancestry
```

The reference group is defined on *other* ancestries on purpose. Taking people whose focal estimate
is near zero is circular — those are the ones the caller got right, so the floor measured on them is
biased down, and most in exactly the cohorts where the focal ancestry is hard to call.

## Step 2 — get the window

```{r eval = FALSE}
th <- adm_threshold(q_hat = cohort$AFR, curve = "AFR", eps0 = eps)
th
#> Inclusion window  [measured curve]
#>
#>   detection optimum    0.00382   efficiency 0.840   keeps 3,705
#>   estimation optimum   0.00568   efficiency 0.833   keeps 2,730
#>
#>   recommended window   0.00382 to 0.00568
plot(th)
```

Two optima, because loosening the window moves detection and estimation oppositely: more individuals
shrink the standard error while worsening attenuation. Anything between them is defensible.

## What `curve =` is, and why it is not optional

The closed form has one free parameter and gets the **scaling** right — the optimum moves in
proportion to `eps0`, with a ratio near 1.45 across two decades. It does **not** get the level right.
Checked against a held-out-founder simulation on the same cohort:

| | closed form | measured |
|---|---|---|
| reliability at q̂ = 0.001 | 0.58 | **0.14** |
| detection optimum | 8.4e-4 | **4.4e-3** |
| efficiency there | 0.97 | **0.78** |

A user running the closed form alone would set the cut about fivefold too tight and believe their
efficiency was 0.97 when it was 0.78. So `adm_threshold()` warns when no curve is supplied, and the
shipped curves are the default route.

```{r}
head(adm_curve("AFR"), 4)
```

Shipped curves come from RFMix 2 against the 5-way HGDP+1kGP reference, 16,000 held-out-founder
mosaics. A different caller is a different curve — but it can be moved.

## Using a shipped curve for a caller we did not measure

Reliability depends on `q` only through `q/eps0`, so a curve should move to another caller by scaling
its axis by the ratio of their floors. Tested, on RFMix and FLARE run over the same mosaics, where
`eps0` differs 2.4-fold (1.33e-3 against 3.19e-3):

| q/eps0 | 0.4 | 1.5 | 7.5 | 38 | 150 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| reliability, RFMix | 0.284 | 0.552 | 0.848 | 0.942 | 0.955 |
| reliability, FLARE | 0.255 | 0.574 | 0.848 | 0.943 | 0.952 |

Median disagreement across 0.38 < q/eps0 < 319 is **0.005**. What it costs a FLARE user on a real
52,639-individual cohort:

| window chosen from | cut | efficiency attained |
|---|---|---|
| FLARE's own curve | 7.4e-3 | 0.859 |
| **shipped RFMix curve, rescaled** | 9.0e-3 | **0.858** |
| shipped RFMix curve, unrescaled | 3.8e-3 | 0.843 |

```{r eval = FALSE}
cur <- adm_rescale(adm_curve("AFR"), eps0_from = 1.33e-3, eps0_to = eps)
adm_threshold(cohort$AFR, curve = cur)
```

Two things follow. Rescaling is a supported route, so an unmeasured caller does not force a full
calibration. And the choice is **forgiving**: efficiency near the optimum is a plateau, so a twofold
error in the cut costs under 0.02. Quote the window to one significant figure.

Validated on one caller pair, one focal ancestry, one reference panel.

## Reproducing the two published windows

On the UK Biobank cohort the package returns 3.8e-3 (AFR) and 5.4e-3 (SAS) against the 4.4e-3 and
2.6e-3 obtained from the per-individual scores directly. The difference is binning: the shipped curve
averages `a` and `w` within q̂ bins and interpolates, where the direct computation keeps every
individual. AFR lands within 15%; SAS within a factor of two, which is enough to pick a window and
not enough to quote to two digits.

## What this does not do

It optimises the two-ancestry non-centrality parameter. Contamination by a *third* ancestry is a
different axis and is handled in the scan — by adjusting for the other ancestries' local dosage per
window — not by the inclusion window. Narrowing the window to reduce third-ancestry contamination
costs information for no gain in that respect.
